Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise before the House today on the occasion of International Day to End Violence Against Women.
Violence against women may be the most pervasive yet least recognized human rights violation. It is a problem common to virtually all countries, cultures and classes. However until recently it received little international attention.
I am proud to advise the House that Canada is one of the leading nations addressing the problem. Earlier this month at the United Nations in Vienna Canada sponsored a meeting of international experts to consider means to eliminate violence against women. The meeting strongly recommended that the UN adopt a declaration on violence against women to set out measures to address the problem.
I can assure the House that Canada will continue to take a leadership role internationally to develop measures to counter this pervasive problem in order to ensure that women are able to live free from fear and violence.

November 25, 1991
Oral Questions

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Quebec's cultural community is greatly disturbed by the Arpin report recommendations that the Canadian government should withdraw from the cultural sector. People in the film, television and publishing industries, including producers, directors, technicians and authors of books, films and videos, with their colleagues in the recording industry, as well as many members of the Union des artistes, totally disagree with this approach.
The arts community in Quebec is well-known here and abroad. Its creative spirit and talent reflect the diversity of our society. However, the vast majority of its members recognize the fact that their energy and enthusiasm would no longer be the same without the financial contribution and the sustained and indeed necessary support of the Canadian government.
That is why I hope members of this House and members of the arts community will explain to others the advantages of the federal government's contribution to arts and culture and urge the government to maintain its contribution intact.

speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier this month the media reported that the government might be considering a fee to be paid by returning Canadians at the border. My immediate and public reaction was: Over my dead body.
I wrote a letter to the Minister of Finance to that effect. The minister knew of my strong opposition to such a surtax. We do not need a fee which will unduly increase the workload of our customs officers and run counter to our efforts to move the traffic at the border. What we need are initiatives to address the underlying causes of our uncompetitiveness, federal measures that complement and supplement those which need to be undertaken by the private sector and our provincial counterparts.
For a few weeks the minister made me sweat it out. I could not sleep at night. I was on the edge of my seat. My wife said I was more irritable than usual.
Finally last week I met with the Minister of Finance. At the meeting the minister gave me his assurances that the federal government would not proceed with this cross-border levy.
On behalf of my friends, my family, my staff and my constituents the message to the Minister of Finance is thank you: "Thank you, Mr. Minister, for this breath of life and this momentary peace of mind".

Today, the number of children living below the poverty line in Canada is greater than the entire population of Nova Scotia or Saskatchewan. These children are Canada's future. Does the government intend to act and do something about a problem as the House of Commons had asked it to do two years ago?

This may include both children at risk and other child-oriented issues. However, the Leader of the Opposition knows perfectly well that this is above all a matter under provincial jurisdiction. Perhaps he could ask the hon. member for Hamilton East. I imagine her leader would care to listen, and if she would have the decency to listen when we are talking about children, she might understand these issues.
November 25, 1991

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a supplementary question of the minister.
In the last election the government made a very clear promise to have a national child care program. As I said earlier, the population and the children who live in poverty in Canada would fill the Toronto SkyDome 200 times.
We read in the paper this morning that the government is waiting to introduce this program at a time when it will be closer to an election. These children cannot wait for an election, they have a problem right now.
I want to know from the minister when this promised program will be introduced. It has been three years, almost to the day since the election was held.
Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health
and Welfare): Mr. Speaker, I repeat what I said. I said it has nothing to do with the election. Before January we should be able to produce a strategy for children, having in mind what has to be countered in a program for children today, particularly sexual abuse, children's place in the family, violence and so on.
I also said we will consider the question of child care. The Leader of the Opposition was told yesterday by specialists that we should not spend money we do not have. That is the first reason for poverty.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we learned yesterday that it is possible to have prosperity in Canada and to make sure at the same time that it is possible to keep the people of Canada and the poor in dignity. This is what we learned yesterday.
I have a question for the Minister of Finance. Four thousand people in Cape Breton took to the streets to try to save the economy of their region. They do not want any more of these fly-by-night operators who come in, get money from the government and then go with the cash and do not leave any jobs behind.
Oral Questions
I want to know from the Minister of Finance when we can make sure that the people of this part of Canada, who were protesting over the weekend, will get what they want, jobs. They do not want handouts, they want dignity, jobs, and they are waiting for this government to act accordingly.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I want to congratulate the hon. Leader of the Opposition and his party for entering the real world of global reality. I followed to some extent the discussions that went on with his senior people who were talking about the future.
Globalization is a fact of life. Canada is a part of the global economy and it is necessary for us to get our fiscal house in order. It is necessary for us to make the structural adjustments and changes, be it in tax reform, be it in trade policy, be it in implementing a GST, which replaces the old federal sales tax which was a silent killer of jobs, be it the free trade agreement. These are the kinds of initiatives that will bring about long-term prosperity and economic durability and that is the policy of the government.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Yesterday in eastern Nova Scotia thousands of people participated in a march of concern to draw attention to a national crisis of unemployment in Cape Breton and the horrendous number of welfare claimants.
Jobs and dignity were their slogan. Now, on their behalf, I ask the government for the government's assistance. Will the Minister of Finance direct senior officials of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency to meet with municipalities, business and labour to put in place an emergency employment program for Canadians who reside in that region of the country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister responsible for ACOA is in the Atlantic region every weekend if not every week. He meets with interest groups, he meets with people who are interested in new job opportunities, new economic opportunities and he is there to lend a helping hand.

Oral Questions
If the hon. member has any specific suggestions to advance to the hon. minister responsible I would be pleased to convey that to him.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would remind the minister that the unemployment situation in Cape Breton is a national crisis.
People have lost their dignity and families believe the future is extremely bleak. But Cape Bretoners, as Canadians in that region, have not lost the hope that they can make a meaningful contribution to Canadian society.
Therefore, I ask the Minister of Finance if he, in co-operation with the minister responsible for ACOA, will order their federal agencies, CEIC, Enterprise Cape Breton and ACOA to meet with business, labour and municipal representatives to put in place and implement a plan before we adjourn this House at Christmas. Will the Minister of Finance give that undertaking?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is absolutely no need to give any orders to that effect to officials of ACOA or to officials of these other departments because they already know what the task is. The effort to create employment and jobs in Cape Breton has doubled since 1984. The amount of money spent in overcoming regional disparity has gone up by a tremendous amount.
In Cape Breton, for example, since the ACOA program started, the authorized contributions to economic development have been $75 million and $253 million has resulted in project costs. Extraordinary efforts have been made through Enterprise Cape Breton and in other directions in Cape Breton.
Very often we hear criticisms that we are taking too many chances down in Cape Breton and not the reverse.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance who will be meeting with a large delegation of prairie farm leaders tomorrow, leaders who are here not only because
farmers have no money but because they face a debt problem of Third World proportions as well.
Since 1982, the value of farm assets on the prairies has fallen by $20 billion. Prairie farm debt stands at $12 billion, with no income to cover it. Since over 24,000 prairie farmers went bankrupt or became insolvent last year, will the minister stop this devastation of the farm community by placing a moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation foreclosures immediately?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is very much aware of the trade war that is going on wherein farmers in Canada find themselves in a squeeze.
We have responded not only this year but in previous years. There was a poll that reflected that fact this week where over 90 per cent of the farmers that were surveyed indicated that they are only in business today because of the support that has been given to them by the Government of Canada. That is continuing.
In so far as his suggestion about placing a moratorium on the Farm Credit Corporation foreclosures is concerned, we have a process in place through the Farm Debt Review Board which I think has worked very satisfactorily. It has not been perfect but it has provided a mediation approach where farmers can sit down and work out their credit difficulties with independent people serving as arbitrators. I think that process has worked very well because to provide a moratorium has consequences as well.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
I know the government has dished out a lot of money and I know that a blizzard of discussion is going on but the truth is that at the same time the FCC is out there like the grim reaper, mowing down farm families right across the prairies.
Will the minister do what the Agriculture Credit Corporation in Saskatchewan has done and announce an immediate freeze on all FCC foreclosure actions so that there will be some farmers left when this farm crisis is finally resolved.
November 25, 1991

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member has any examples of unjustifiable actions taken by the Farm Credit Corporation against farmers, I wish he would bring them to my attention or the attention of the Minister of Agriculture because I am sure he would be very interested and we could certainly deal with those issues.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Finance. Since two farm families are forced off the land every day, the system is not working. A much larger and long-term solution needs to be found.
The Government of Saskatchewan will be attempting to formulate a solution and will be inviting the federal government as well as the private financial institutions to meet together to work out a better long-term solution. Can I get a commitment from this government to fully co-operate in that effort so that we can find a long-term solution to the farm debt and to the whole question of the intergenerational transfer of land?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is aware, I am sure, of the debate which took place earlier in the House. We have established the GRIP program and the NISA program, the Gross Revenue Insurance Plan and the Net Income Stabilization Account which is broad legislation that not only provides assistance today but down the road. It will provide stabilization for the future. This is a long-term approach to providing support and stability to the agricultural community.
I think the hon. member, who tends to criticize that particular approach, would do well to review that particular program and its effectiveness because even now as I speak money is flowing to the farmers under the Gross Revenue Insurance Plan as well as the Net Income Stabilization Account. In addition to that, $600 million plus in emergency financial assistance was provided this spring, plus another $800 million worth of emergency assistance was provided this fall which is in the process of being distributed before Christmas.
Oral Questions
Surely, Mr. Speaker, we have in place the permanent types of programs as well as the ad hoc programs to help farmers in this time of need.

OCCUPATION OF CANADIAN EMBASSY IN HAITI
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many Canadians are worried about the occupation of our embassy in Port-au-Prince which has been going on for days.
I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister why, after a week, the government has been unable to take control of the situation. Why not ask for the help of a third party, such as the churches or international organizations, in putting an end to this occupation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: OCCUPATION OF CANADIAN EMBASSY IN HAITI
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there really has been no change in the situation. We have said to those who are occupying the Canadian embassy that it would be in their best interests to leave as quickly as possible, as peacefully as possible, so that no harm would come to themselves and no further damage would be done to our embassy. That is a position which has been supported by President Aristide and by the Haitian community in Montreal.
Once again we would say to them: Leave our embassy as quickly as possible.

subtopic: OCCUPATION OF CANADIAN EMBASSY IN HAITI
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the situation is becoming ever more confused. The Prime Minister in Paris last week said that the situation is in the process of being resolved in Haiti, that the return of the Aristide government seems to be totally uncertain.
The embassy has been occupied now for over a week. I want to ask the government and the minister, what makes the Prime Minister so optimistic. What kind of additional measures is the government taking to end the occupation? In particular, can the minister tell me if the delegation of the OAS which will be in Port-au-Prince today will undertake to address the stand-off in the Canadian embassy and use their good offices to end this occupation?

November 25, 1991
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: OCCUPATION OF CANADIAN EMBASSY IN HAITI
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has not been a week as yet since the occupation took place. I think the best approach with this type of situation is to send a very clear and unequivocal message to those who are illegally occupying the Canadian embassy that they should leave peacefully and quickly and enable us to return to business as usual.
The delegation which is obviously involved with the OAS has other issues which they are addressing. At this point we continue to maintain the position that those who occupy the embassy should leave.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Deputy Prime Minister concerning child poverty and the House's resolution on the matter.
The group called Campaign 2000 announced this morning, in trying to implement that, what they saw as principles. I wonder if the Deputy Prime Minister would agree with their version of the obligations of Parliament. Does he agree that the federal government has the paramount responsibility to finance national programs, to maintain national standards and to create a framework with provincial governments for the development and implementation of national strategies to eliminate child poverty?
Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health
and Welfare): Mr. Speaker, I said before that we are working first with the provinces concerning child poverty and we will continue to do that.


I refer my friend to the $6.7 billion in programs which we put into the system every year. Moreover, if we consider all the tax credits and all the tax cuts that we have for Canadians it comes to about $15 billion a year. I do not say that it is too much, I say that it is a lot of money and it is done in light of the capacity to have to do that.
We are looking for a package which will allow us to find ways to do more.
Once again I repeat, Canadians have to know that the costs of programs dealing with children and families are one-tenth of the Canadian budget. It is not too much but I believe it is the second highest level in the world.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the minister.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 52 I rise to ask for an emergency debate to bring to the government's attention the urgent need for it to fulfil its promises to alleviate the current Canadian farm crisis.
November 25, 1991

The government knows that at least $1.3 billion is needed to address the farm net income shortfall resulting from the continuing decline in net farm incomes.
Last month it agreed to provide 60 per cent of this minimum requirement in the form of an $800 million aid package.
Farmers already in crisis learned this week that the $800 million commitment was somewhat diluted by being divided into two equal parts, $400 million transferred from the unused allocation for the gulf war and $400 million in the next fiscal year for a new requirement on corporate taxpayers to submit one-half of income tax funds in dispute. The second half of the government's commitment is being postponed until the next fiscal year.
On top of this, last Friday farmers learned that an 11 per cent cut had been made to the funds promised for this year. Only $356.2 million of the $400 million promised was transferred in the supplementary estimates that were tabled on Friday. The government may not fully understand the gravity of the situation facing Canadian farm communities or the critical need for it to provide all the funds promised. Urgent action is required. There is little time for the government to reverse the erosion of its aid package and provide new supplementary estimates.
I submit an emergency debate would provide the most timely and effective means for this House to bring the concerns of Canada's farm communities to the attention of those with the means and the responsibility to address them.

He said: Mr. Speaker, there are three motions that are grouped here, Nos. 5, 53 and 55. You have read Motion No. 53. No. 53 is very basic to the position of this party with respect to financial institutions.
Throughout the study and the restructuring of financial institutions, we have held as a basic principle that the wide ownership which now applies to banks is the best hedge against the concentration of power. We wanted that to be extended to all other financial institutions. We have been concerned. There are many Canadians, informed Canadians, who are very concerned about upstream, non-financial ownership.
In other words, we are concerned by the Standard Trusts of this world, financial institutions that are owned and controlled by individuals or companies that have nothing to do with financial institutions. In this particular case, Standard Trust, it was an uranium mining company which owned the financial institution. We now know the problems that have been caused by this ownership.

In fact, very informed people such as Mr. Corrigan in the United States, who is very informed on the regulation of financial institutions, has recommended strongly that we ought to keep the commercial and financial operations separate.
We know that in fact the whole matter becomes very involved when you have relationships at the top where decisions for the owning company affect the assets of the financial institution.
We believe that it is the best way to prevent any kind of less than arm's length relationships. We have also provided, in Bill C-5, an amendment which we believe is important in that the government, in the Bank Act, and in Bill C-4 said that governments ought not to establish banks.
The federal government is prohibited from starting a bank. I want to say that this certainly reveals a medieval view of the state. To actually prevent the federal state from starting a bank, it seems to me is to cut out the option of the ownership by people of a banking or a financial institution.
Provincial governments in Canada do own trust and loans companies. Right here on the Sparks Street Mall there is the Ontario government's Provincial Savings and Loans. In Alberta and in other provinces they own savings and loans companies.

I pointed out that it seemed to me rather medieval that the federal government would not be allowed to own a bank.

I think the improved legislation that we have before us today deals with and addresses the concerns that the member has about self-dealing. This legislation, C-4, contains the 35 per cent rule for companies. That means that 35 per cent of the trust company has to be publicly owned if it has over $750 million in capital. There is a ban on self-dealing. There are audit committees. There are conduct review committees. These are some of the measures that are in this legislation to eliminate selfdealing.
I feel the concerns are taken care of in C-4. The Superintendent of Financial Institutions and the chairman of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation are two people who are extremely knowledgeable in this area and have indicated that this amendment is not necessary.
In Canada we have a mixed regime of closely held and _ widely held financial institutions. I think that mix has ' served us well over the years. The Canadian government has not had to spend one dollar bailing out uninsured depositors of a closely held financial institution.

A final point I want to make is that it allows smaller companies to be closely held but it requires them, as they get larger, to become more widely held. If you look back in history it is mainly the smaller companies trying to break into the market that fail and not the large ones.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a few words in support of Motion No. 5, specifically clause 22 of Bill C-4.
This amendment would remove the prohibition in the bill against the incorporation of a company by Her Majesty in right of Canada or in right of a province or an agency thereof.
In this country we seem to be almost horrified at the prospect of the government being in the commercial banking business. There seems to be a widely-held view, particularly on the political right, that governments cannot in any way efficiently operate a banking system, or at least a bank.
I do not know how this has come about. I do not know whether it is influenced from the United States or whether it is our own ingrown thinking processes. But one only has to take a look at, for example, banks in France or Germany or Italy, not all of which are state-owned or nationalized. Certainly in France, for example, many of which were just recently nationalized, not under a socialist government. It was begun even before Francois Mitterrand became president. But, nonetheless, they were nationalized. As far as I know, and I admit I am not an expert in the field of banking, the French economy is not on the skids because the major banks in that country are state-owned. That is not the reason why the French economy may be on the verge of a recession today, for example. There are many other reasons.
In Canada we do have at the federal level the Federal Business Development Bank. It is called a bank but it is really only a half-bank or a near-bank or a watered-down kind of bank, because it is not allowed to receive deposits and it is not allowed to enter into many other activities that the chartered banks enter into in their daily course of business.
Originally the FBDB, which was set up in the mid-1970s, was a bank to extend credit where primarily the private banks or the chartered banks were afraid to go. They did not want to take on unnecessarily high risks so the FBDB was there if you had certain assets or, if it had some faith in the borrower, it could charge a higher interest rate and it would lend money. I think it has to be in excess of $250,000, which is unfortunate. We all have constituents in this country who come to us from time to time wanting to start a small business. But the commercial banks or the chartered banks refuse to extend small loans to them in the amount of maybe $50,000 or $75,000. We send our constituents to the FBDB and they are told they can lend them nothing less than $200,000 or $250,000. Of course, for an entrepreneur just starting out with very limited assets and capital, that amount of money is horrendous in his or her imagination and planning. Then they come back to the Member of Parliament and say: "Well, thanks very much but I was turned down, not because I asked for too much but because I asked for too little", or perhaps for some other reasons.
I do not know why, in a bill such as C-4, we should deliberately prevent the Government of Canada, or any subsequent Government of Canada, from going into the commercial banking business. I do not know what the reason is. Is there tremendous opposition from the chartered banks at the present time, and they want it both ways? They do not want the Canadian government to be in the banking business. They want to control it, but they also want to make absolutely certain that some of these riskier individuals are not allowed to borrow small sums of money for business ventures.
I do not know what their motives are. I have not talked to the banks or any bankers recently about this. It seems to me that the FBDB as it is presently chartered is damned if it does or damned if it does not. For example, if the FBDB makes good loans, the Canadian Banking Association will accuse it of straying away from its mandate as the lender of last resort and steal the business in the process from the private banks. They will also claim that the bank is an unfair competitor because of its cut rate loans, if the loans are made at lower than commercial rates. Incidentally, this is a claim that is unfounded at the present time.

The FBDB is only an unfair competitor to loan sharks because it has been systematically lending at rates varying from 1 per cent to 3 per cent above normal rates. That is one need that the FBDB may fulfil at the present time. But I would like to see the federal government, through this bill, have the opportunity at some future date, if not at the present time, to revamp the FBDB to make it a national bank, a government bank, competing with the private banks. Perhaps it could keep the private banks or the commercial banks or the chartered banks just a little more honest. Maybe it could make them a little more competitive. I do not know today whether or not the banks are competitive. You go to four banks on four different street corners and you are going to get virtually the same interest rates on deposits and moneys borrowed. I do not see where the competition is, quite frankly. I do not know where the choice is. You talk about freedom of choice in this country as part of the right wing agenda. I do not know where the choice is in interest rates, quite frankly. They are minuscule, if they are there at all.
What I would like to see is a bank that goes where no other banks have gone before: in the small loans field, where we are at least willing to take a risk. We have a government that wants to promote small enterprise, small entrepreneurship in this country, and yet these days every conceivable obstacle is put in the way of people going into business. We have very high bank rates. We have banks that demand that you have so much collateral to begin with so they can grab it if you go down. They want collateral to the point where if a business did have that collateral, it would not have to go to the bank in the first place to borrow the money. It is this kind of ridiculous situation that I think we have to try to reform and change.
I am supporting this amendment under Motion No. 5. I hope that the government will come to its senses and at least make provision for this government or subsequent governments to expand public banking in this country.
I see nothing wrong with this kind of banking, for example, as I said at the outset, in countries like France, Germany and Italy. I do not know why we should be so special in this country to be so fearful of government owned banks, one government owned bank in this country that would act as a true competitor to the chartered banks.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few words of support to this particular amendment that would make it possible for a government to go into the banking business. It is certainly not any great skill and it would not mean that every government would have to do it.
I can recall when the New Democrats were the government in the province of British Columbia. We felt the need to have some bank that represented British Columbia and we did not feel that the existing banks were doing it in the way we wanted it done, but it was totally impossible under the legislation as it now exists. This amendment would make it possible. At one point, we were considering the possibility of acquiring a bank that was for sale in the United States and moving its head office to a point just immediately south of the 49th parallel so that it would still be in the States, but at least it would be a bank identified as one that was serving the interests, as we saw them, of the people of British Columbia.
Of late, there has been a lot of criticism of the banks, for example, for having almost a common interest rate when it comes to credit card dealing. If a bank, under the ownership of the provincial government, wanted to be the leader in setting those rates at what the government thought was a more reasonable rate, then that could be done. With that kind of competition I suggest it would not be long before the other banks would see the need to follow suit lest this way of handling things spread across the country.
It would not be totally new. The previous speaker talked about the Federal Business Development Bank which is in the banking business to some extent but is not able to take advantage of the many opportunities that are there for banks to cover the costs of making loans that are sometimes a little riskier than others.
The federal government used to be in it in a way too when we had the post office savings accounts. I think, Mr. Speaker, you will remember when that was a feature of life here in Canada, when people could go to the post office and do a good deal of their banking through the post office accounts such as making savings, but there were certainly limits as to what they could do. They were anything but full banks, but at least the government did set up that possibility. Post offices in those days, before Canada Post took over, were in many small communities throughout the country where banks were not available and it was not convenient for people to get to them.

We are not saying that a government would have to do it. We are not saying that the federal government would have to do it or that any provincial or territorial government would have to get into this business. If any government felt the need to do it, it could use that perhaps as a way of persuading the existing banks to do something differently or could even establish a provincially owned bank or purchase a bank to get into the banking business on a relatively modest scale. It would at least show to the banking industry how the government felt it should be operating in a way of providing a better service to the people of the community, to the people of the provinces and to the people of the country than it was already doing.
It is just making it possible, without breaking the legislation, without circumventing it, as we were thinking of doing in buying a bank outside of the country and moving it close to the border of British Columbia. There would be no need then to adopt this subterfuge, this way of achieving what we wanted to achieve on behalf of the people of British Columbia.
We had investors ready to make substantial deposits in it. It was our plan at the time to get involved a lot more in housing loans, to encourage home construction. A lot of homes need building in British Columbia. I suppose it is the one bright spot in the economy of B.C. right now. British Columbia is one of the leaders in the country largely, I believe, due to the fact that we are doing a lot of residential construction to accommodate the people who are fleeing to B.C. from many other parts of the country. Retiring, I think, more than fleeing.
It gives the governments the opportunity to do this and to act on behalf of the people.
If the people do not like what the government is doing, they will have the opportunity one, two, three or five years down the road to show that government what they think about what it is doing and get rid of it. They have the final say and they have the opportunity to change the government and to even stop the government from embarking on such plans and bringing it to fruition if it has not gone that far, or getting out of that business if the people of the province or of the country think it is not in the interests of the people.
I support this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I too wish to speak in favour of the amendments in front of us today.
First, one of the amendments relates to the ability of the federal government to enter into the banking business. In the Bank Act there is a prohibition against the federal government entering into the banking business, meaning the federal government is not allowed to become a deposit taking institution.
We do have the Federal Business Development Bank, but that is not a deposit taking institution. We have seen that institution, which can and should be helpful, particularly to small businesses, not being very active at all. The few small business people I have talked to who have had some experience with this institution do not speak very highly of it. To become embroiled with it very often means to become embroiled with a whole slew of bureaucrats and it is not really fulfilling its mandate, which is to help the small business community and to help those businesses particularly where commercial banks have not been all that helpful.
We hear small business people when they make their presentations to Parliament and to the finance committee continually complaining about the type of treatment they get from commercial banks. Certainly if we had an effective bank that was in direct competition with the commercial banks I think there would be much better treatment by our commercial banks to the small business people, particularly those who are trying to start a business.
The other amendment we are dealing with and that is grouped together refers to the sliding scale in terms of ownership and size.
I remember when I was on the finance committee and we tackled this one back in 1985 or 1986. There was the request of the trusts to be treated equally with the banks, but we had to tackle the question of ownership. One person or institution cannot own more than 10 per cent. That is not the case with the trusts.
At that time it seemed to make some sense to us to have ownership based on a sliding scale. The argument, for example, of a small trust company in Nova Scotia that was a sort of family run business requiring a new set of ownership rules that would prevent the family from owning 50, 60, 80 or 90 per cent of the trust, and if that trust were to become like a bank, to only allow that person 10 per cent ownership, did not make much sense to us and I think rightly so.
November 25, 1991

If memory serves me right, I thought the finance committee was in agreement with that. If it is a small trust, then you allow one person to own 100 per cent, or whatever. If the trust got bigger and bigger you would require that the ownership be more widely distributed so that if the trust got to a certain level-I do not remember the figures off hand but we are talking about the concept-and wanted to be treated like a bank, then it also had to comply with the regulations that no one individual or institution can own more than 10 per cent of that trust.
There were reasons why banks were restricted in terms of the ownership to no more than 10 per cent to an individual or to a particular institution. The reason is that no one family or person or company can control a bank and manipulate through total ownership its functioning for their own business interest.
That is why philosophically we are opposed to the linkage of commercial interests with the financial deposit taking institutions.
Again, the fundamental reason was the protection of the public interest. This is fundamental. Every amendment that we are introducing to this act is based on the basic premise of public interest. We heard our critic, the member of the New Democratic Party for Nickel Belt, this morning read into the record the comment of my comrade and former chairman of the finance committee, the hon. member from Mississauga, who in his sometimes flippant but very honest manner described the situation as "a done deal".
All the co-ops, all the banks, all the life insurance companies and all the trusts sat down and made the deal. When he read that, the question that came to my mind was: who was representing the public interest in this deal making? Who sat at that table and said: "Hold it a moment. This and this from a public interest point of view does not make sense?"
I am afraid when we see this particular government introducing changes to our financial institutions that are so fundamental. We know it is of the same political stripe of the presidencies of Mr. Reagan and Mr. Bush. We have seen the public interest being degraded south of the border. I am afraid we are seeing the public interest being degraded here north of the border.
Government Orders
Where is the public interest? Who is there to protect depositors, the public? I am not saying this to be melodramatic but who is there to protect the widow and her life savings or the young working families that have put their life savings in deposits in these financial institutions? They are trusting that these are solid institutions, and that when they retire so many years later these institutions will still be around and their savings and their deposits will be well managed in their interest. They trust their deposits will not be managed in the interest of some financial or commercial organization, but in their interest.
That is fundamental. If you break the public trust in our financial institutions, forget about the financial institutions. We are back to the primitive days when people were putting gold underneath their mattresses.
I am afraid that with some of the proposals contained in this legislation, even though I am sure the life insurance companies, the banks and the trusts are going to be very happy, in the long run they will undermine the public trust in those institutions and therefore work in the end against the interest of those very same financial institutions.
Again I repeat if the public trust is no longer in those financial institutions, then those financial institutions will be the first to suffer. We saw in the 1980s major falls of trust companies in this country. We have seen major deposit taking institutions south of the border totally being wiped out.
They say it is going to cost up to $1 trillion in the United States to bail out the savings and loans. That is taxpayers' money. Talk about deficits. That is taxpayers' money. Where was the public interest? Who was there to protect the public interest when that occurred? Obviously, they were not there. They were asleep at the switch.
I am afraid, with some of the proposals in this legislation, we are opening ourselves up to those same types of mistakes.
In discussing further amendments, I will reiterate many of these points and elaborate on them as well.

The hon. member for Nickel Belt.

Mr. Speaker, I think you have to understand what is envisaged by this particular motion. We on this side of the House have taken the position that banks should do the things that banks best know how to do and that insurance companies should do the things related to insurance matters. Similarly, trust companies should do the things related to trust and loan companies, and co-operatives in the same fashion.
We have opposed every attempt to collapse the pillars. When this bill is all done it is going to allow banks to own insurance companies, insurance companies to own trust and loan companies, and banks to own trust and loan companies. I have no hesitation in saying that when this is all passed you are going to see the greatest urge to merge ever in this countiy.
We have taken the position that we ought not to go for that approach. The sumo wrestler approach is not the one that we should be aiming for. We have said that there is nothing wrong with a bank entering into an agreement with an insurance company, a joint venture, and for the bank to market the insurance products of an insurance company or several insurance companies. Already banks do insure. There is creditor insurance and banks do market insurance. There is mortgage insurance and banks do market mortgage insurance. We have said quite frankly to banks: "You cannot market insurance out of your branches, but you can go ahead and set up your own insurance company or buy one of the smaller insurance companies and start building its base".
It seems to me that this is not serving the interests of consumers. All this will lead to when it is all said and done is that one morning Canadians are going to wake up and there will only be one super financial institution with arms like an octopus.
When we dealt with Bill C-83, which is the former name of C-4 in the previous Parliament, we came to clause 416 and lo and behold we looked at the French version of the clause and the French version says that you cannot do anything except what we tell you to do. The English version said: "You can do anything, except what we tell you not to do". At the time we felt that the natural person's concept was reflected in the English version. I moved to change the French version so that it was more consistent with the English version. All the members on the committee agreed to that.
I want to say that the beloved chairman of our committee flew off to Toronto and spoke to a meeting of insurance brokers and insurance companies.
In Thiwan?
It was not in Taiwan. He did it in Toronto.
Did they feed him lunch?

It was a supper meeting. Lo and behold he came back like he was on some safari to Damascus. He was a converted man. He said "You cannot do this. Now you have broken the deal". Now the banks would be able to dipsy-doodle around the rules laid out in Bill C-83, now Bill C-4, and market insurance.
In one fleeting moment, one shining moment, in a committee room on Parliament Hill, parliamentarians decided that what was a done deal was not what we thought ought to be. In other words we decided to show our political and economic masters that they can no longer keep us on this chain. We were going break the chains that bound us to the towers of finance in this country. They were not allowing us to have that little crumb. So, they hauled our favourite chairman down there and he came back a changed man. He said: "You cannot do this because you would have broken the done deal".
November 25, 1991

I want to get back to this done deal because it is very important for people who are watching to understand. In the committee this is what the chairman said to me. I want to put it on the record.
The chairman said: "I know where we are going here and you all know where we are going. Let us face it, this deal is a cut deal. Is that what you are saying you have negotiated? You have had representations from all sides and essentially, this is a must situation as far as your minister is concerned". Mr. LePan from the department says "yes".
The chairman is not satisfied, he has to nail it down. He goes on to say: "As far as the minister is concerned and the government is concerned, from all sides, essentially, this is a must situation as far your minister is concerned". Mr. LePan says, "Yes".
"As far as the minister and the government is concerned, you want the legislation this way". Mr. LePan says: "That is right".
It seems to me the way that works is if the boys over at the towers at the CBA want this and the insurance people want this, what does our favourite chairman say? "Aye, aye, sir". And what does the minister say as he looks at the member for Mississauga South, since he probably knows more about than the minister. He says: "What do you think"? He says: "Aye, aye, sir".
For one moment we decided to do this. In this particular clause we decided that the natural persons' approach was the correct one. Lo and behold in Bill C-19, the government acceded to the requests of their financial and political bosses and turned around and are now saying: "You have to change C-4 back". I want to tell you this member and this party are not for turning. I want to tell you that my colleagues did a lot of turning up at Aylmer over the weekend. They turned 360 degrees on many, many important issues and I suppose they are going to turn on this one too.
That is the background behind our motion. We have absolutely no objection to banks marketing insurance through their branches as long as they are not allowed to own insurance companies. We believe that is the way you can provide better prices for consumers at the grassroots
Government Orders
level. This important aspect of financial matters should not be left in the hands of the insurance companies which would be owned by banks. You would then have a concentration of ownership and prices would never come down.
We believe that banks can deliver this service to consumers much more economically and in a wider way because they have all of the branching networks across the country which insurance companies do not. That is the argument for this motion.

Mr. Speaker, certainly this amended version of Motion No. 57 is one that I will be supporting. After a great deal of study on the financial institutions and a great deal of thought, we feel that banks and trust companies should not have the power to sell all types of insurance.
I will be speaking at third reading in great detail on that, but today I will give three or four reasons. Actually there is no evidence to show that banks can really sell insurance cheaper to customers in the long haul.
Second, to give banks power to sell insurance could be very unfair competition for the insurance industry. The Royal Bank has assets of $126 billion. That is more than all the assets of the insurance industry put together. So we are very concerned about the possibility of very unfair competition.
There are also avenues to suggest that there could be some tied selling, where a bank will say to a customer: "We are not going to give you a mortgage unless you buy your insurance from us". There was a study done in the United States which showed that there are certainly situations where tied selling does exist.
Those are basically three of the reasons which I will detail on third reading.
There is a question that I find hard to understand, listening to the words from the hon. member of the NDP. Why does he want banks to have all the banking functions and also sell insurance, but only wants insurance companies to do insurance? I have to ask you, Mr. Speaker, whether that is fair. I certainly do not feel that it is and I will be supporting the amended version of Motion No. 57.

Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I certainly wish to enter the debate on this particular section as well.
It revolves around, and we debated this way back in 1985, the ability of financial deposit-taking institutions like banks to sell and get into the insurance business. Of course, the fundamental problem is that if you go to a bank for a mortgage the bank is going to say: "Hey, we have this package for you. You have to take this insurance. You have to take this life insurance. You have to take this insurance on your house". There will be some connection there. You have to go and get your mortgage, so you are sort of forced into taking all these other insurance policies. Of course people say: "No, no. We are going to protect the consumer from that".
When I was attending the finance committee meetings, it used to be called the china wall. Apparently now it is called the fire wall, although I understand that the fire wall is going to become more like a wall of fire. You cannot regulate against that. You cannot enforce the regulations.
You have a little office somewhere in Strasbourg, Saskatchewan. There is the Royal Bank of Canada or whatever and you go there. You want to get your mortgage. Right beside the loan officer is a guy selling for the insurance company that the Royal Bank of Canada owns, as an example.
These two men or women are working beside each other. They are going to have lunch together.
They cannot do that.

You cannot do that. Of course, you cannot do that, but who is going to stop them from doing that?
Can we trust this government- which believes in getting off business' back and allowing business to do its thing, that everything will turn out rosy-to enforce these particular regulations?
The funny thing is that in these proposals that the government is bringing forward we are going to need more regulations. The government is going to allow things that will tempt the devil. Therefore we are going to need more regulations to prevent that.
To tell you the truth, I do not believe in the ability of this particular government to enforce regulations. It does not believe in regulations. The Conservatives are the bunch that says deregulate.
We can build up a nice regime that works well on paper. We have the regulations in. We have got the regulators out there. We have the inspectors out there and lo and behold the political winds shift and we have this new right wing neo-Tory government. It gets elected on the notion of take government off the peoples' backs, deregulate, clear it up.
Hear, hear.
We hear "hear, hear". They can hardly restrain themselves from yelling "hear, hear".
Wait until Preston starts pulling the strings over there.

Yet the whole regulatory regime that is being established by the legislation the government introduces depends upon an effective regulatory body. We are asked to believe in this House that this government, these people across the way, these neo-Tories who yell "hear, hear" at the mere mention of deregulate, is going to put in place an effective regulatory body.
Give me a break. Is this a joke? Do they really expect the people of Canada to believe this? Come on, Mr. Speaker.
They would believe in the tooth fairy too.

Mr. Speaker, it is in the public interest to maintain the pillars. Let the insurance companies do what is best, sell insurance. They have their agents and they have developed their marketing. They have agents all over this country. I believe the Canadian public has been well served.
To throw all those people out of work and make them redundant so that the banks can start selling insurance is not going to help the consumer or the insurance industry in this country. I do not think it is going to be in the interest of the insurance industry either to become involved in a deposit taking institution.
The insurance industry has served Canada well. Let it be. There is no need to meddle in something that is working relatively well. Do we want to follow the American example? Is that what these Tories are so hot to trot about, to become like the Americans? They just had horrendous failures in the savings and loans institutions. Do we have to become like the Americans and have more failures here as well? Are the failures to be picked up by the Canadian taxpayer through deposit insurance and perhaps direct outlay of public expenditures?

The old saying is: "If it is not broken, don't fix it". We believe when it comes to providing good insurance policies to Canadians we have done well, and let us keep it that way.
I cannot support the proposals of the government. I cannot believe that this government will set up an effective regulatory regime, that it will have the people capable of doing that or the funds and the resources to be able to do the job, or that it will have the resources to do the proper regulatory job that this legislation is going to require.
It cannot be done by a group of neo-Tories. We have a group of neo-Tories in government today. It is a contradiction of terms. What the government is proposing here and what is going to be required to make this effective and real cannot be done by a group of neo-Conservatives. It cannot be done. I stand opposed to the motions of the government.

speakeroldname: Mr. John R. Rodriguez (Nickel Belt) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 30.
That Bill C-4 be amended in Clause 204 by adding immediately after line 4 at page 102 the following:
"(3) The Directors of a bank shall place before the shareholders for approval, at every annual meeting, a list containing the names of the five directors, officers or employees of the company who are to receive the highest salaries to be paid by the company in the next financial year of the company, together with the amount of such salaries.
(4)	Notwithstanding any Act of Parliament, the salaries referred to in subsection (3) may be paid only to the extent that they have been approved by special resolution.
(5)	Forthwith after each annual meeting of shareholders, the company shall send to the Superintendent, a list containing the names of the five directors, officers or employees of the company who are to receive the highest salaries to be paid by the company in the ensuing financial year of the company together with the amount of such salaries.

Motion No. 47.
