"(3) A person who in good faith makes an oral or written communication under subsections (1) or (2) shall not be liable in any civil action arising therefrom."
November 25, 1991

I have waited for this for a long time, Mr. Speaker. Basically this amendment is what our country is all about. It is what we in the western world have always held to be the ultimate, and that is democracy.
From the whole experience I have had with financial institutions, I have found that what we want for our country and what we uphold as a model is democracy. Lo and behold, those corporate entities of this country fall far short of the model.
In fact that was one of the major purposes for moving this. I mean this was the first opportunity I had in dealing with banks and financial institutions. Shareholders are provided the opportunity to vote on the remuneration of the board of directors, but those same shareholders are not provided the opportunity to vote on the salaries of the highest paid officials of the particular institution, whether it be a bank, a trust company or an insurance company.
It seems to me that the shareholders ought to know what these people, their employees, are being paid. It is like saying to the people of Canada that they have no right to know what public servants earn or they have no right to know what MPs are paid. After all, the people of Canada are our shareholders, and God knows they have this information available to them because this is their company.
This is their government. This is their Parliament. They are paying their share in the cost of running the country and they want to be able to know what is going on. It is only fair.
I hear a lot about the fact that we want to create a level paying field with our major trading partner, the United States. The executives of large companies in the United States have to file their wages with the Securities and Exchange Commission. We have no such thing here. When we want to find out what a Canadian corporate leader is making, we have to go to the United States. If that company is doing business in the United States it has to file there. That is where we find out the information. For example, we find out information about Don Phillips, President of Inco Ltd. We have to go to the United States to find out he makes $1.9 million a year. Raymond Cyr of Bell Canada Enterprises makes $1.2 million a year. Frank Stronach makes $1.2 million a year.
Government Orders
Arden Haynes, chairman of Imperial Oil, makes $1.2 million a year.
It is important that shareholders and investors know the salaries being paid to the chief officers of their financial institution.
The Ontario Securities Commission is holding hearings to find out if this information should be revealed. It has received some 58 briefs and the vast and overwhelming majority of these briefs say no. It is absolutely astounding that for some reason some people do not believe that their wages should be revealed to the shareholders of their company.
They point out that should this information be revealed they and their families might be more subject and susceptible to kidnappings. For example, I am not aware of any statistical information showing that people from Forest Hill are more often kidnapped than people in the working class communities of Toronto. Another respondent to the commission said he does not want this information released because he does not want to be bothered by all kinds of people trying to get him interested in buying stocks and making other kinds of investments.
No one is obliged to be a senior corporate executive in this country just as no one is obliged to being a member of Parliament. It is a choice you make. With respect to what the government is doing to the economy of this country I wish it felt more obliged to listen to the Canadian people.
I believe it is in the interest of the public that the salaries of the top officials be known. We started a hearing on Standard Trust and we found out some very alarming things with respect to the kinds of deals which have been made to pay bonuses to executive officers. They were based on how many commercial mortgages they could generate, how much of the company's money they could lend for mall development, et cetera.
It seems this is one of the ways the shareholders have in controlling what is going on at the top of their company. After all, it is their money that is being spent.
I have taken the opportunity in this amendment to put this in. This is not just titillating pornography for the public. This is important business for the shareholders and the investors of the company.

Government Orders
It seems to me that we, as the federal government, could take the lead. We could send a clear message to those provincial organizations, such as the Ontario Securities Commission, that are presently contemplating bringing in some rules to reveal this. Surely the argument that has always been made is the one that says: "We have to be more like the United States because we have to compete in its market". How is that all the good regulations and rules it has we never want to adopt, but all of the more questionable measures it has in legislation, by golly, we want to adopt them here willy-nilly?
I argue for this particular Motion No. 30. I hope the House will see the reasonableness of it and the need for it and will vote for it.

Mr. Speaker, this is an issue that we read and hear a lot about from time to time.
I must say that during the committee meetings when we were discussing the financial institution legislation, there was not one witness who brought that up. It appears to me that it really is not a very pressing matter in the minds of shareholders.
I know that the hon. member for Nickel Belt mentioned the Ontario Securities Commission was looking into this and had briefs. No doubt we will be hearing from it that it will be making a decision later this fall.
I know that there are some people who argue that wage disclosure would put shareholders in a better position to assess the fairness and reasonableness of the allocation of resources. They also argue that investors should know if executives are receiving too much in the way of salaries in regard to the profit the company is making.
On the other side of the argument, there are people expressing concern for greater privacy, personal risk and that there would be increased competition which would raise salaries.
This amendment was put forth by the New Democratic Party. It is far from certain whether this amendment will discourage higher executive salaries in Canada. I believe that is what the party hopes.
It is interesting to note that the U.S. law on which this amendment is based has reportedly not discouraged higher salaries there. Rather, it has encouraged higher salaries. When the top five salaries are disclosed some executives will undoubtedly look at them and figure out that they are underpaid. We could have the same situation happen in Canada in which the CEO of Royal Trust would find out that the CEO of Canada Trust is making $100,000 more. What would happen? The CEO of Royal Trust would want more money. That is what has been the experience in the United States with this law on which this amendment is based. It has really driven salaries up, not down.
In view of that, this is an amendment we will certainly be voting against.

Mr. Speaker, the naivety of the previous speaker is overwhelming on two points. This amendment is not primarily to try to keep executive salaries down. That is a matter for the various corporations to wrestle with. As far as the chief executive officers of one company not knowing approximately what the salaries of the chief executive officers of another company are, this is absolutely ridiculous. Of course they know. They do not know down to the exact penny or dollar or hundreds of dollars, but they certainly have a very clear idea of approximately what the top directors and the top CEOs are getting. As a matter of fact, if their stock is traded on any of the American exchanges all they have to do is phone Washington and they can find out immediately.
The point here is that it is a matter of principle. I do not know why there should be boardroom secrecy on this kind of issue. I do not know why we write laws in this country deliberately prohibiting or denying shareholders the right to know what their chief executives are earning. It is as simple as that. It is a matter of principle. It is a matter of openness.
I want to give an example of what happened in my community a number of years ago when the Canadian government and the government of the province of Ontario gave Massey-Ferguson Corporation $200 million in an attempt to get that company back on its feet; $125 million from the federal government and $75 million from the province of Ontario.
November 25, 1991

We in Brantford wanted to know what the then chief executive officer of that company was earning and we could not find out and the Government of Canada could not find out and the government of Ontario could not find out. Yet taxpayers were being asked to cough up $200 million to bail out that company. We had to go to the United States to find out what Victor Rice was earning. If memory serves me correctly I think he had taken a decrease in pay from something like $275,000 a year to $245,000 a year as his great contribution in helping to bail out that company at the same time that the taxpayers were giving him $200 million.
It is a matter of principle. We believe in an open society in this country. We believe in open government, although not all parties practice what they preach when it comes to open government. Here we have a wonderful opportunity in this House, legislatively, to make certain that shareholders and the general public and the Government of Canada know what the salaries of these chief executive officers are.
The other point is it is manifestly clear that chief executive officers do not want their employees to know and do not want their shareholders to know what their increases are year over year, when in periods of economic recession their employees are being asked to take less. There is the other side of the sword. Maybe some chief executive officers in the last couple of years have only had a 4 per cent or 5 per cent increase. Maybe some have had a 7 per cent or 8 per cent increase. If you add their perks and their privileges and the stocks that they get and the entire package then you may find that they are getting a hell of a lot more than 4 per cent or 5 per cent increases year over year during a recession when they are demanding from their employees maybe a 2 per cent or 3 per cent increase or maybe a 0 per cent increase.
Why not the openness? Why is the government defending the chief executive officers of the major financial institutions of this country against their own employees? That is the question and that is the principle.

Mr. Speaker, my friend from Nickel Belt who brought this amendment brings it, I think, with a great deal of intensity in his understanding, but it is really an amendment that has something to do with stocks and stock trading situations on a stock exchange. He will know that the regulation of
Government Orders
security companies is a provincial matter and, properly, the Government of Ontario is conducting hearings on this issue.
What we have here is a situation in the way we run trust companies and remember, trust companies are trust companies. They are very much, in detail, supervised by the Superintendent of Financial Institutions. The salaries paid to all of the officers are known to the Superintendent of Financial Institutions. But they are a matter that ought not to be public. It is important in the solvency arrangements we are trying to protect for the Office of the Superintendent that as much confidence be there in financial institutions. That confidence should not be eroded by debates as to whether the salary of an officer is too high or too low or whether it compares with another company or how it fits in the pecking order. That ought not to be there because that kind of a debate attacks the credibility of the institution.
We have a lot of provisions in this bill in connection with the election of directors, to make directors very responsible for the management of the financial institutions covered in this group that we are going to be dealing with.
With respect to trust companies, a great number of them are relatively closely held. The owners know what they are paying their chief management people. They know it very well and they are hiring the best people they can, at the best price they can. The superintendent knows what they are paying them because if they are paying them too much, the superintendent will treat that as he does any matter that comes before him concerning the solvency of the institution.
So we are not dealing with a situation of Massey-Fer-guson Ltd. and Mr. Rice or an Inco and so on. These are not situations where shareholders have a great deal to gain by the information. Indeed, the shareholders have a great deal to lose by the information because they want their company to be successful and managed well. They do not want their company to have its linen spread across the street to cause problems with the nature of their company and the value that they have in their investment.
The government believes that the proposal is not appropriate in a loan and trust company bill. It is not appropriate, indeed, in any of the financial bills, and so the government cannot support the amendments.

November 25, 1991
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak in favour of Motion No. 30 by the member for Nickel Belt. Before I talk about some of the parts of that motion, I want to deal with the rather odious and foul-smelling arguments put forward by the member for Mississauga South and the member for Malpeque.
The member for Mississauga South, publicly in this House, has always patted himself on the back as being someone who always favours disclosure. The public's right to know is what he has branded himself on the forehead as being the great saviour of and the great promoter of all across this country. And here, on an amendment that would simply reveal the salaries of the top five paid executives of corporations, he is saying no, no, no. The hon. member will not explain it, but he tries to throw out a little bit of a boomerang, a little bit of a curved ball, a little bit of a smoker, when he says it has something to do with stock trading. He will not be specific, he would not go into it, but he said that the government cannot tell us what any of the CEOs or any of the top salary earners are getting because it has something to do with stock trading.
The member for Malpeque reveals the Liberal oyster, so to speak. I guess they really did slide to the right over the weekend. Her argument is that this could lead to competition for higher salaries. This is going to be known in the next federal election as Malpeque reasoning. Here is the reason you cannot disclose anything; it could lead to higher salaries. You cannot have that. That will probably be the argument the Liberals will use for not telling what the members of the Senate make, or anyone in the House of Commons, or what you pay for taxes, or what it costs to take the bus. It sounds to me like the kind of thinking that probably brought about the demise of the Soviet Union.
Let us take a look. One of the points raised by my friend from Brant is very important. We know why the National Citizens' Coalition likes to kick members of Parliament for the amount we are paid and everything else. They want to bring down the credibility of public institutions.
Have you ever heard the National Citizens' Coalition talk about the fact that the principal beneficiaries in every corporation in the country have hidden salaries?
Not likely. We know who funds the National Citizens' Coalition. We know why they continue to attack public institutions and why they are after the Public Service Alliance of Canada and Daryl Bean right now. We know why the NCC is doing that.
I see the Solicitor General here today. I am sure he is going to speak. He says he knows why the National Citizens' Coalition is going after the Public Service Alliance.
Viewers like to know what goes on in the talk box. Let us take a look at the amendment because it is a good one. It would amend clause 204. It says that the directors of a bank shall place before the shareholders for approval at every annual meeting a list containing the names of the five directors, officers or employees of the company who would receive the highest salaries to be paid by the company in the next financial year of the company together with the amount of such salaries.
It is interesting that the Liberals and Conservatives, who are always a team, are arguing that we cannot have that. We certainly could not possibly have the directors of the bank doing something like that.
Then it goes on to say that notwithstanding any act of Parliament the salaries referred to in subsection 3 may be paid only to the extent that they have been approved by special resolution. The member for Mississauga South is always talking about disclosure and the right to know where the buck is spent and that the buck has to stop somewhere. One would think he would be the first one to stand on his hind legs and argue vigorously and vociferously for there to be a paper trail from the shareholders to the directors to the salaries that are being paid to the top five.
Why is he cozying up? Is he going to leave with the Minister for International Trade for the Bank of Nova Scotia? I am always amazed after elections when government members are defeated. You can always tell the ministers who were really out there cutting the deals. They are in the paper day after day for weeks after the election, appointed to the board of blinkety-blank corporation, and blonkety-donk, and dinkety-dank, and stin-kety-stank. It just goes on and on. Look at the list of some of them; guys like Peter Lougheed with 40 or 50 directorships. What about Bill Davis?

We are obviously drilling on the right teeth. It is like being in a dentist's office. I can tell when they are getting a little jumpy over there. You can tell when you are getting close.
It says further that forthwith after each annual meeting of shareholders the company shall send to the superintendent a list containing the names of the five directors, officers or employees of the company who are to receive the highest salaries to be paid by the company in the ensuing financial year of the company together with the amount of such salaries.
That is basic fundamental disclosure. I doubt that there are many members in this House who do not from time to time contact the U.S. Securities Commission to get that kind of information either on new corporate entities operating in their constituencies; on ones that are already there; when there is starting to be a feeling about things in Alberta and you want to check things out. You might just want to make a few calls and find out how much dough is moving up and not down. That is what shareholders like to know. They want to know when those five CEOs have the plunger on the bank account and they are sucking it up into their offices. You want to know because that is how a lot of shareholders have been stripped of a heck of a pile of dough in this country.
The hon. member goes on in point six and says that for the purposes of this section, salary means any form of remuneration payable by a company for work performed by a director, officer or employer of the company. It includes-because this is where a lot of these corporate sharpies have discovered ways to get stuff under the rug, and I am not talking about dust-commissions.
They might get a little commission on a trip. It might be 10 grand, 20 grand, 30 grand.
How do we know about vacation pay and bonuses? I would not want to use the PM as an example. Let us say somebody wanted to pay him back for a big deal such as a free trade deal and he got a big chunk of property in Florida.
I am saying that in that situation, the people of Canada would eventually find out. What if it was one of the CEOs of a big corporation cutting a special deal? It could be a deal with iron ore. You shut down this town and we
Government Orders
will give you a bunch of dough later. We will keep it off shore in a bank.
Disclosure is fundamental to public trust. What about bonuses? Bonuses are quite often paid after the fact. You do the dirty job and you get it 12 months later. All of this kind of stuff should be made very clear and disclosed.
The stock options, too.
This guy Munk. There is a word that rhymes with that, when one talks about the money he made on the gold shares. What did he make, $5 million or $50 million?
$50 million.

Thanks, Bos. That is right. Bosley might have had some of those shares.
All of this kind of stuff should be disclosed well in advance so we know exactly what kind of dough these guys are hauling away in their Loomis trucks to their vacation homes.
Reasonable value for rent and housing: that is another good burial ground for special perks for the top five in every company. They get a nice house, say, a $3 million or $4 million house. They just live in it. They get a few rugs thrown in. They just hang around in there. They get it rent-free.
The shareholders should know about this kind of thing and they should not be Malpequed on it. This is not a situation where the oyster has to clam shut. I do not want to mix my shellfish metaphors, but I do not like oysters that clam up.
I think we should toss out that Liberal argument that disclosure could lead to higher salaries. I cannot wait to put that in my election material. "Payments of any kind".
I am just getting to the good stuff in this section. "Payments of any kind: Any other advantage received directly or indirectly from the company." That is where you really have to start looking. I think that is why Johnny properly put it in there.
We want to get to the bottom. We want the dirt on these guys who are up at the top monkey wrenching our economy, monkey wrenching employees and hiding all sorts of things from the shareholders.

Government Orders
All we are asking is to get out of this colonialist, beaver hat mentality, get both feet on the ground and say: "What kind of dough are these guys getting? What are they taking?"
Mr. Speaker, I can tell from your agitation in the chair that you would love to have an opportunity to get up and vote for this amendment because it is the best one we have heard today.

Mr. Speaker, I also wish to participate although I think it might be very hard to follow my colleague.
In all seriousness, it is amazing that we are still debating this point in 1991. There is not public disclosure of the salaries of the chief executive officers of a public company. I underline the word "public". What is going on here? Why not?
It seems to me that in almost every civilized, developed country, the requirement is there. It certainly is in the United States. Again, it is put there to protect the shareholder. The job of a government is to help protect the public interest including shareholders.
That is why you have public institutions. That is why you have government. That is why you have a public domain. It is the job of this government to ensure that there is legislation so that information like the perks, salaries and remuneration of chief executive officers of publicly held companies is public information.
We generally consider ourselves to be a modern country, and in many ways we are.
Every now and then there are these little dark holes that sort of throw us back into medieval times, into the dark ages. This is one of them. The fact is that there is no requirement in this country for public officers in a publicly traded company to have information about their salaries made public. It is a dark hole.
I am quite amazed at the Liberal Party which really perpetuated this, because it has been in power for years and years and years and never did anything about it. In that period in opposition, it modernized itself enough to be able to support a relatively more modem contemporary regime when it comes to public disclosure.
It has given the indication today that it is going to go along with the conspiracy of silence. The reasoning one hears, whether it is the Liberal Party or the Tory Party,
trying to rationalize something that is irrational, is totally outdated and totally belongs to the dark ages. To hear it squirm and dance around this point is really quite, quite humorous. It would be a laughing matter if it were not so sad because it is serious about it.
It suggests that this is going to encourage high salaries and this is the experience in the United States. How can you make that determination? It is logically impossible to say that it has created higher salaries in the United States. You have to be able to then compare it to a situation in which these rules were not in place. Who knows? Salaries in the United States for the chief executive officers might be 100 times more had that requirement not been in place.
The hon. member from the Liberal Party, looking for a reason in order to impose the amendment, decided to take this particular interpretation. It is not rational mind you, it is just an attempt to try to create some rationality for a decision the Liberal Party has made.
When I hear my friend from Mississauga South trying to justify this and knowing the hon. member, I suspect his heart was not entirely in his reasoning. I know the hon. member is very much concerned about public disclosure. I know the hon. member believes that if the public knows something, in its infinite wisdom it will correct wrongdoings. The key thing in here is public knowledge, public disclosure.
If there is some hanky-panky occurring among the chief executive officers, it can best be corrected by self regulation and the shareholders bringing to task their board of directors. You need public information and public disclosure. The shareholders have got to know what is happening in order to be able to correct a wrong situation. If there is no public disclosure, you cannot really have a correction of any wrongdoing.
There are some real reasons why people do not want to have their salaries exposed. The member for Brant makes the point very clearly that in difficult economic times when everybody is being asked to tighten the belts and to make a sacrifice in order to keep the enterprise going, it is important to know that the chief executive officers are also tightening their belts, that this is just not a cynical exercise in order to deny employees an increase in their salary while the employers are continuing to take larger amounts of various forms of remuneration.

It is important for the employees as well as for the shareholders to know what is being paid. Particularly for the smaller institutions it is important for the shareholders to know that a few of the boys at the top are not really raking it all in. It is going to affect the value of the shares and the amount of dividends that are going to be paid and this is very important for them.
The shareholders will never be able to know unless there is a full and total disclosure, particularly for small and medium sized financial institutions. This is very important because it will have a direct bearing or it could have a direct bearing on the dividends being paid in the value of the shares and in the long run on the health of the financial institutions.
I think the argument in favour of full disclosure is an argument that was made in the States and a reasonable one many years ago. It is amazing that we will have this debate in 1991 in Canada and it looks as though we are going to have this debate perhaps 10 years from now when again the Bank Act is going to come up. Let us hope that somewhere in here some enlightenment and modem thinking will occur and that finally in Canada we will start having public disclosure of basically public institutions. These are public institutions so therefore the public, i.e. the shareholders, surely have the right to know.
It is quite amazing that this government cannot act on behalf of Canadians and on behalf of the shareholders. I find that irresponsible.

Motion No. 47
That Bill C-4 be amended in clause 329 by adding immediately
after line 11 on page 168 the following:
"(3) A person who in good faith makes an oral or written communication under subsection (1) or (2) shall not be liable in any civil action arising therefrom."
She said: Mr. Speaker, I am moving this amendment today because it follows logically from one of the Liberal Party's objectives when we were dealing with this financial institution legislation, and that was to improve the soundness of Canadian financial institutions. It is an objective that we kept in mind when dealing with the various witnesses and briefs and presentations that came before the committee and certainly one that we are very concerned with when you consider what is going on south of the border.
This amendment prevents a lawsuit against anyone who gives information in good faith to an auditor of a financial institution. We feel that protection is important because a free flow of information to auditors helps make for sound accounting and actuarial principles and practices.
We feel that it is a protection that is needed because questionable accounting practices have been blamed in part for the failure of two western banks in 1985 and last year's failure of Ontario based Standard Trust. The Superintendent of Financial Institutions told the finance committee last November that improved accounting practices might have made a difference in the case of Standard Trust.
If an employee of a bank has information that he or she knows the auditor needs or would help the auditor to perform a proper audit, but that the trust company or bank would rather not disclose for various reasons, then that employee might be reluctant to come forward with the information and risk a lawsuit. However, if the employee does have information and he knows that he cannot be sued by the bank-he gives that information to an auditor in good faith; in other words, he is being honest and he is being very sincere-he is more than likely to come forward with it. This new information could result in a better audit, a better financial statement and a better chance for the superintendent to catch small problems before they become big ones that might bankrupt the institution.

November 25, 1991
Government Orders
I would urge the House to support this amendment because I feel it is in the best interest of the Canadian financial institutions.

Mr. Speaker, I very much recognize the motives behind the member for Malpeque and I very much approve of what she has been saying.
The problem, though, is that I think the amendment is not necessary and presents a danger in society when we absolve people from civil liability for what they say.
Clause 329 of the bill says that employees, agents or servants of the company, officers, former directors and so on, shall provide information to the auditor if the auditor requests. The company, under subparagraph (b), shall provide information that the auditor requests. These are mandatory obligations on employees, officers, agents, directors and former directors of the company to provide information to the auditor.
When you are required under a statute to provide something you are required to provide it. If the auditor cannot get the information, his job is to go to the superintendent and demand the superintendent enforce that obligation as set out in the statute. But surely we ought not to go one step further as my friend would suggest and absolve people from any liability they might have in a civil action.
I do not want to go into the details or possibilities that one could imagine in a civil action. Surely you cannot be subject to a civil action if you are required by statute to supply something. But if you supply far beyond what you are required to do, if you do things that deliberately injure a company, then maybe you should be responsible for what you say and do and maybe you ought to be subject to civil liability in a civil action.
I think it goes too far to say that you can somehow slither out of your responsibility to be forthright and your responsibility to say what you want to say, by somehow being excused from civil liability and then able to plead: "I mean, sure I slandered them but I am excused". If what you are disclosing is what the auditor requests then you are okay. Surely a reading of the statute is that way. But to go on beyond that and allow people to escape liability for commercial slander, because they decided to go far beyond in their own view or disclose more than
what was really required as a court may determine and to make statements that are damaging to a company because of a disclosure made on the request of an auditor, seems to us to be beyond what we ought to allow and beyond the protection we ought to give to people fulfilling their requirements under the statute.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in support of this amendment. As I read the amendment I compared it to the clause in the bill it is purporting to amend. The provisions in subclause 329(1) and subclause 329(2) talk about present or former directors, officers, employees or agents of the company and about the directors of the company.
It seems to me that this amendment provides much more surety so that when an employee reveals practices that are not consistent with the rules governing the operation of a financial institution, they cannot find themselves facing a civil suit because they did the right thing. They revealed to the Superintendent of Financial Institutions or to a member of Parliament or to the minister certain things that were not going correctly.
I think for example of Standard Trust. God knows we ought not have depended on Diane Frances with respect to Standard Trust, because a year before the bottom fell out of it she was touting Standard Trust as the best investment going. God knows she has poor financial judgment and she has poor political judgment, for that matter. She had poor economic judgment in suggesting to her readers that they ought to go out and invest in Standard Trust, in other words not having looked at the company thoroughly.
Suppose some employee of the company had revealed to an editor of a financial paper certain things that were going on in the company, certain bonuses being paid for going out and rustling up mortgages to mall contractors. Let us assume that that sort of thing was going on and that was revealed. I think this motion puts an onus on citizens to reveal things that are not right. In fact, if this government had any kind of courage at all, it would bring in whistle-blowing legislation that protects people in the Public Service. It took the PSAC organization to establish a telephone line where people can phone when they think things are being done that are not consistent with the rules established by Parliament.
November 25, 1991

Government Orders
It seems to me that the last time a fellow tried that in Canada Post he lost his job. As a matter of fact he had blown the whistle to a Tory and the Tory went out and fought the good fight for him. Then, lo and behold, the Liberal government was defeated and the Tory government came in and here was the post office under a Tory department and they kicked the guy out. There was one hell of a dust-up to get this guy back his job.
Watch that language.

One dust-up for the guy to get his job back. It seems to me that this amendment puts an onus on citizens, people who work for financial institutions, that when they see something going wrong-and God knows we need it now-or something that is not in accordance with the rules, they ought to be able to blow the whistle and not be afraid of finding themselves facing a civil suit.
That has happened. That is one of the most effective ways companies have of shutting up their employees. That is one of the most effective ways of continuing this conspiracy of silence. I have to support this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak in favour of this amendment proposed by the member for Malpeque. Over the last decade I have made a number of attempts to get whistle-blowing legislation through this House without much success under either Liberal or Conservative regimes. Yet jurisdictions all over the world are adopting it because when one does any kind of a cost benefit analysis of the kinds of information one gets, one realizes pretty quickly, particularly in the field of health and safety, that there are enormous benefits to the public to having whistleblowing legislation.
This proposed clause could be included on page 168. Let us take a look specifically at the section where it is to go. In the column it is described. First there is the auditor's examination, clause 328. Then the auditing standards, then right to information. I think this is what any shareholder or any member of the public would be interested in.
It says:
On the request of the auditor of a company, the present or former directors, officers, employees or agents of the company shall to the extent that such persons are reasonably able to do so,
(a)	permit access to such records, assets and security held by the company or any entity in which the company has a substantial investment, and
(b)	provide such information and explanations
as are, in the opinion of the auditor, necessary to enable the auditor to perform the duties of the auditor of the company.
It is pretty clear it is covering present and past directors, officers, employees or agents of the company. Then it goes to directors to provide information, an obvious consequential clause which says:
(2) On the request of the auditor of a company, the directors of the company shall to the extent that they are reasonably able to do so,
(a)	obtain from the present or former directors, officers, employees and agents of any entity in which the company has a substantial investment the information and explanations that such persons are reasonably able to provide and that are, in the opinion of the auditor, necessary to enable the auditor to perform the duties of the auditor of the company; and
(b)	provide the auditor with the information and explanation so obtained.
The amendment proposed by the member for Malpeque says: "A person who in good faith makes an oral or written communication under subsections (1) or (2) shall not be liabled in any in any civil action arising therefrom".
As the member for Mississauga South or the minister or members on the government side would know, there is in the courts a broad range of definition in terms of good faith. Something cannot just be made up and given in written or oral form during an audit and suspect that if there is following litigation that you are going to somehow or other be protected because you are a nice person or you wear blue shoes. That does not fly. You have to be able to demonstrate that you provided that information in good faith and that you, in fact, thought the books were being cooked or something was being jigged or the widgets you were making were not being shipped. You need some foundation in reality in order to be able to use the good faith argument.

November 25, 1991
Government Orders
I think the member for Malpeque has quite properly brought this forward. It is not a broad based, whistleblowing concept but it does provide, in a general sense, the kind of balance that one wants. You do not want an employee, for whatever reason, to say that because they did not get a raise or they did not get an appointment to something they wanted, they would then use the next available opportunity to be involved in some kind of scurrilous, under-handed, improper attack while an audit was going on. At the same time, you do not want to foreclose the likelihood that someone with valuable information, particularly as we watch what has gone on in the United States or in western Canada, for that matter.
Let us keep in mind what has been going on in a lot of financial institutions. Some of it is clearly tied to the Reagan deregulation policies that were implemented and created an enormous fiasco in the United States. We know what has caused some of the serious collapses in this country.
There are people, often at very junior levels in many financial institutions in positions of public trust who know there is something going wrong, whether it is simply in an area of bookkeeping or in an actual area of commodity or financial transfers. I think we need not just this wording but additional active areas of whistle-blowing to touch on pieces of legislation such as this in its broadest sense. We need to protect the person who gets his pay cheque, goes home, pays the rent, pays for the bike for the kid and pays for maybe a swimming lesson a month, pays for some clothes, pays for the groceries and then has nothing left. There is the prospect of being tied up in civil litigation and because of their economic income they might not be eligible for any kind of legal aid. They have to think: "Gosh, if I tell the auditor this and I get sued by Mr. X who does not like me very much anyway, I am going to end up with all of these additional costs, not only to have a lawyer, but what if I lose".
I do not think any longer at this point in the 20th century it is a sign of good government to simply bury this kind of wording and say: "Well, now, we just cannot have it". I listened with care to what the member for Mississauga had to say and I do not buy the argument.
I think anyone who has been around the courts, around whistle-blowing situations, as we all have been on the government or on the opposition benches, knows the kinds of pressures that Canadians operate under, particularly in financial institutions where you are constantly dealing. Think of the pressures on the prairies right now between people who work in financial institutions and farmers. Twenty-four thousand have lost their farms in the last 12 months. Two a day are going into financial institutions absolutely, totally gone. They have lost their homes, their tractors, their machinery, their cars, their dreams. They have lost everything.
Within those financial institutions there are all of these other pressures that are constantly there. Without this kind of wording, all that it is is a protective shield. It is not a wall. It certainly would not protect anyone who for ill purposes or ill reasons provided inaccurate, improper or false information. What this does, and it has a good foundation in common law in this country and under British common law, is provide some kind of protection.
One can only continue to wonder out loud during debates such as this why the government would not want to have that in there. Why does it not want it in there? It is just one more unnecessary piece of protection for the very wealthy, the elite, the bankers and the super rich. Why is there always special protection for those who already can afford to hire a lawyer, another accountant or another auditor.
But no, the government says: "No. We have to give them one more kind of protection, one more coat of veneer to make sure that they can never be caught up, whether they have been doing things properly or improperly, legally or illegally". What the intention of this clause is, and I stand to be corrected by the member for Malpeque if I am wrong, is where there are situations where there may well have been wrongdoing is to open that window so that a little bit of fresh air can come in and that person directly or indirectly involved with the information would say to themselves: "I know I am right. I studied those records. I helped produce those records. I dealt with that farm foreclosure. I know what is going on. What I have been seeing in the papers and hearing around here is not what really went on in that branch. I am going to go to the auditor in good faith as is provided".

We have the auditing standards, the auditor's examination, right to information and directors to provide information. Why should it not go that one extra step to where I consider the mother lode of accurate information to be, which is among the employees at the lower end, not at the $100,000, $300,000, $500,000 salary level where they do not do any of the direct monkey wrenching. They are the ones who know. They deal with the $10, $100, $1,000 transactions. They are the ones who know because they see the roots. If there is some kind of funny business going on, that is where we need to be able to follow the trail.
I think it is incredibly short-sighted and narrow minded for the government not to agree to support Motion No. 47.

Mr. Speaker, I too wish to join in the debate on this amendment and congratulate the Liberal Party for introducing a good amendment. I am glad to see, despite the stance that they have taken on some other very worth-while amendments, that they have come forward with something that I can support.
Certainly when one discusses financial institutions, banks, life insurance companies, trusts and so forth, one sees the true colours of the political parties being revealed. One sees the Tories standing up and protecting the interest of private wealth and private capital to quite an extent. As my colleague from Skeena has pointed out, why do you give this extra piece of protection to the very wealthy, the people who can hire their own lawyers? They do not need this extra piece of protection. The government, darn it, when it comes to the wealthy is going to give them every break possible.
The opposition to this amendment I do not quite understand. Let us step back and see what the government is doing. It is collapsing the pillars. It is bringing in a new regime in which banks can sell life insurance companies, trust companies can be controlled by banks, commercial interests can control deposit taking institutions. It is all going to be one. It recognizes that there is a possibility of conflict of interest here between the life insurance part and the casualty insurance part and the mortgage part, and so forth, and there might be possibilities of conflict between the commercial part and the
Government Orders
deposit taking part. The government is setting up and is going to have to set up a regulatory regime. In remarks I made earlier this afternoon, I expressed my grave concern of how a neo-Conservative government can really set up a proper regulatory regime to make certain that there will not be conflicts of interest.
The Tory rhetoric very often is: we need self-regulation, let them be self-regulatory and let the industry regulate itself. If they were really sincere about that, the best way to ensure some form of self-regulation would be to accept the amendment that is being proposed today. It would make it easier to remove the type of pressure, the type of blackmail fear that the large financial institutions can place on a lowly clerk such as the fear of having to face in court, with all of its expenses, some charge that some hot shot lawyer in Toronto in one of these huge towers in the bank zone is going to bring to bear on that little individual. That lowly individual can see that there is a conflict occurring and knows that the person who is giving the mortgages is unofficially insisting that a certain life insurance policy and mortgage insurance policy be purchased. The lowly little clerk has to run up the numbers and enter it all into computer and begins to see some correlation between the commercial interests and the interests of the deposit taking institution. To allow that individual to alert the proper authorities that something wrong is happening would be a tremendous arm in the process of self-regulation. It would ensure, where wrongdoings occur, that they can brought to the attention of the enforcers of the regulations.
I have grave doubts about whether you are going to have a big enough army of bank regulators to ensure that in Strasbourg, Saskatchewan, at the Royal Bank of Canada, for example, the person issuing the mortgage is not going to also insist, or sort of insist-it does not have to be done officially-that if you want your mortgage "we do have this good insurance policy here". No bank regulator is going to be able to sit down and have a cup of coffee with the person selling the insurance and the person dealing with the mortgages. The lowly little teller might begin to pick up on the fact that certain requirements in reality are being enforced here: if you want that mortgage you have to take out this particular insurance policy.

Government Orders
I think it is essential to allow that lonely little teller to blow the whistle. They cannot blow the whistle with no protection. They are intimidated. Only a very few and veiy brave will blow the whistle on wrongdoing.
If they are given some protection, as this amendment begins to do, then I think those in the banking industry, the life insurance or the trust industry will think twice. In fact, they might even be a little stricter with their employees in saying: "Look, let's make certain we have no tight selling here". They will never know whether the little lonely clerk might not one day say: "Hey, this is too much. This is wrong. I am going to blow the whistle on this".
That is the type of regulation we need and therefore, Mr. Speaker, I urge the government to support this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, in the normal course of consultation and the excellent representations made by members of the New Democratic Party and members of the Liberal Party, including my friend from Malpeque, I have spoken to my friend from Malpeque and suggested that if in Motion No. 47 we eliminate the word "therefrom" at the end of that motion and add "from making the communication", we believe that the motion could be supported all around. It would be a worth-while addition to the bill.
On the same point of order, Mr. Speaker, there is some sense in the arguments presented and it would seem to me on that basis the motion would then read:
"(3) A person who in good faith makes an oral or written communication under subsections (1) or (2) shall not be liable in any civil action arising from having made the communication."
I do not have the material in writing at this point but I believe it is about six o'clock, Mr. Speaker. May I call it six o'clock? Perhaps the paperwork could be organized to present the amendment tomorrow as we continue the debate on this clause.
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, could I suggest to the member for Mississauga South "any civil action arising from such communication"?
